name: Kele
confidence_why: Ross 2002, working from Smythe's 1958 vocabulary and his own data, finds Kele primary stress lexically unpredictable, and Smythe 1970 also calls stress phonemic, the two differing only on whether vowel length or stress is the underlying contrast and how far final stress is the default.

catalog_quote: Smythe believes that vowel length is phonemic and that a penultimate long vowel attracts stress away from its default position on the final syllable. However, his vocabulary and my own data both suggest a different solution. Four patterns occur in disyllables, shown in the following examples ... cvcv́c /pihín/ 'woman', /aháy/ 'N.W. wind', /tehé/ 'fill (TR)', /buéy/ 'crocodile'; cv́:cvc /pí:ron/ 'heavy', /pá:puy/ 'grandfather, grandson', /ká:nuw/ 'main rafter'; cvccv́c /arwán/ 'blue', /putléw/ 'hunting spear', /puskón/ 'dry', /limpáy/ 'thigh'; cv́ccvc /púrkal/ 'sago food', /páŋkap/ 'snare, trap', /dénŋoy/ 'nasal discharge'. The fourth pattern is rare and probably consists mainly of historical compounds (thus /dén-ŋoy/ is 'faeces of nose'). The overwhelming majority of items in Smythe (1958b) have one of the first three patterns. What the four patterns suggest is that primary stress is lexically unpredictable, and that vowel lengthening takes place only when stress falls on an open non-final syllable. If this is so, then vowel length is not distinctive, but stress is. Several facts speak in favour of this interpretation. First, there is never more than one long vowel in a word. [p.128, sec. 1.2] Stress is marked where it does not fall on the final syllable and has been recorded in the data.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Copies checked (extracted text of pp.140-164 of and (1) Ross 2002 'Kele', sec. 1.1 'Phonemes, phonotactics and stress', printed p.125 (p.142): the quoted passage is present verbatim in the text, lines 125-138 ('Smythe believes that vowel length is phonemic and that a penultimate long vowel attracts stress away from its default position on the final syllable. However, his vocabulary and my own data both suggest a different solution. Four patterns occur in disyllables.. If this is so, then vowel length is not distinctive…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In Kele (mostly disyllabic (C)V(C)(C)V(C) words) primary stress is lexically contrastive between the final syllable (cvcv́c /pihín/, cvccv́c /arwán/ - the commonest patterns) and the first syllable (cv́:cvc /pí:ron/, rare cv́ccvc /púrkal/); a stressed open non-final vowel is phonetically lengthened, so length is derivative of stress. Final stress is the unmarked/default position (Smythe's rule; Ross marks stress only when non-final). Smythe 1970:1232 independently: stress phonemic, tends to fall on long vowels, on the penult of reduplicated forms, on the final syllable of noun stems before possessive enclitics, otherwise on the final syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: 1SG possessor noun forms end in a final open vowel 'usually stressed and often phonetically long' (p.126); vowels in unstressed syllables before the stress tend to delete, also in V1 of nuclear serial verbs (pp.128, 138); a handful of length/stress mismatches in Smythe's vocabulary (/-pa:hrán/, /pésey/, /púpuy/, /a:dút/) which Ross suspects are mistranscriptions or compounds; rare cv́ccvc items are mostly historical compounds (/dén-ŋoy/); monosyllables: no length contrast.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, based on citation forms in Smythe's 1958 vocabulary (~1500 roots, Buyang village) and Ross's elicited data; possessive-suffixed nouns and nuclear serial verb complexes behave as single stress domains; polar questions carry rising intonation on the last stressed syllable (sec. on interrogatives).
new_statements.identity_note: Both sources describe Kele as spoken at Buyang village, inland eastern Manus (Smythe's 'Gele?'; Ross adds speakers from Buyang and Tingou). Same language as Glottolog kele1258 / ISO sbc; Ross notes the Schoolings lump Kele with Kurti, Ere and Lele as 'Ere', but the sketch is Kele proper.

readall_conflicts: No new source could be opened, so no new disagreement. The one existing tension in the record stands: Smythe (1970 note 13 p.1232, as already held by the project in, and as paraphrased by Ross 2002 p.125) treats stress as phonemic but tending to default final placement with a penultimate long vowel attracting it (a weight-sensitive-with-final-default analysis, dependent on phonemic vowel length), whereas Ross 2002 p.125 rejects phonemic length and concludes that primary stress is lexically unpredictable with four disyllabic patterns (cvcv́c, cv́:cvc, cvccv́c, cv́ccvc) and that stress is marked in the orthography only where it is not final (p.128). Smythe & Z'graggen 1975 would presumably repeat Smythe's analysis, but this was not checked because the work was not obtained.

sources.note: Sec. 1.1 'Phonemes, phonotactics and stress' p.125: reports Smythe's view (default final stress, penultimate long vowel attracts stress) and re-analyses: four disyllabic patterns cvcv́c, cv́:cvc, cvccv́c, (rare) cv́ccvc; 'primary stress is lexically unpredictable.. vowel length is not distinctive, but stress is'; 1SG possessor forms end in a stressed, often long, open final vowel (p.126); pre-stress vowels tend to delete (p.128); sec. 1.2 p.128: stress marked in the sketch only where it is NOT final. No secondary stress described.
